children: Tata Sampann and ready-to-drink beverages drive growth in India, while Tata Starbucks reports its fifth consecutive quarter of positive same-store sales growth

Tata Consumer Products reported an 18 per cent year-on-year increase in consolidated earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) to Rs 794 crore in the September quarter of FY27, outpacing its 14 per cent revenue growth as the company's India growth businesses expanded.

The consumer goods company's revenue from operations rose to Rs 5,661.13 crore in the second quarter, compared with Rs 4,965.90 crore in the corresponding period last year. Consolidated net profit attributable to owners of the parent increased 15.7 per cent to Rs 469.30 crore from Rs 404.46 crore a year earlier.

Total income grew 13.9 per cent to Rs 5,699.70 crore from Rs 5,003.91 crore in the year-ago quarter. Profit before exceptional items and tax rose 20.8 per cent to Rs 632.28 crore, against Rs 523.28 crore in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal.
The company's Ebitda margin improved to approximately 14 per cent from 13.5 per cent a year earlier.
Tata Sampann, RTD Beverages Drive India Growth

Tata Consumer Products' India branded business recorded underlying volume growth of 11 per cent during the quarter. Its growth businesses, which include Tata Sampann, ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages, Capital Foods and Organic India, grew 40 per cent and accounted for 38 per cent of the India business.
Tata Sampann recorded 57 per cent revenue growth, supported by higher volumes in its core pulses and spices categories, alongside newer segments such as cold-pressed oils and dry fruits.
Revenue from the company's salt business increased 15 per cent, with volumes contributing to the growth.

The RTD beverages business reported 47 per cent revenue growth, aided by wider distribution, premiumisation and new products. Meanwhile, the India tea business reported flat volumes amid subdued category demand. Revenue declined marginally as the difference between volume and value growth narrowed following pricing actions.

Capital Foods and Organic India together registered 15 per cent revenue growth. Shipping disruptions affected their export business, although domestic revenue increased 24 per cent during the quarter. The company introduced 22 products during the period across health and wellness, convenience and premiumisation categories.
International Revenue Grows 7%

Tata Consumer Products' international business recorded 7 per cent year-on-year revenue growth in the September quarter. However, revenue declined 2 per cent in constant currency terms, reflecting a high base in the year-ago period.

In the United Kingdom, continued hot weather weighed on category consumption, although Tetley performed ahead of the category. In Canada, the company reported growth ahead of the category in both regular and speciality segments.

Tata Starbucks reported 15 per cent revenue growth, alongside its strongest same-store sales growth in multiple quarters. The joint venture recorded its fifth consecutive quarter of positive same-store sales growth.
At the end of September, Tata Starbucks operated 505 stores across 81 Indian cities. It added seven net stores during the quarter, including two Reserve outlets.
Management Flags Volume-led Growth And Productivity Initiatives

Sunil D'Souza, Managing Director and CEO of Tata Consumer Products, said the company had delivered its second consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth in FY27, supported by underlying volume growth in India.
He attributed the improvement in profitability to volume-led growth and execution, with consolidated EBITDA increasing 18 per cent during the quarter.

D'Souza also highlighted the contribution of the company's growth businesses, which accounted for 38 per cent of its India business. Tata Sampann and RTD beverages were among the businesses supporting expansion through product development and distribution growth. The company is also deploying artificial intelligence-led initiatives across sales and operations to improve productivity, D'Souza said.
